title: Separation Techniques 1: Revision
subject: Chemistry
description: Elements, compounds and mixtures, solutions, fair tests, and separating mixtures by magnet, filtering, crystallising and chromatography.
author: L.M.

cards.front: What is an atom?
cards.back:
The building block of all matter

(Atoms are the tiny building blocks that everything is made from.)

cards.front: What is an element?
cards.back:
A substance containing only one type of atom

(An element contains just ONE type of atom, e.g. iron, oxygen, sulfur.)
cards.hint: Think: how many types of atom?

cards.front: Define a compound.
cards.back:
Two or more different elements chemically bonded together

(Compounds = different elements CHEMICALLY BONDED. Water [H₂O] and iron sulfide are compounds.)

cards.front: What is a mixture?
cards.back:
Two or more different substances NOT chemically bonded

(In a mixture the substances are just mixed, not bonded, so they can be separated by physical methods [sieve, magnet, filter…].)

cards.front: A particle diagram shows lots of identical molecules, each made of one big and one small atom joined together. What is it?
cards.back:
Compound

(Different atoms joined together, and every molecule is the same = compound.)

cards.front: A particle diagram shows two different kinds of molecule floating around, not joined to each other. What is it?
cards.back:
Mixture

(More than one kind of particle that are NOT joined to each other = mixture.)
cards.hint: Are the different types joined, or just next to each other?

cards.front: How does a PURE substance behave when it melts?
cards.back:
It melts at one exact temperature

(A pure substance has a sharp melting point: one temperature, shown as a flat line on the graph.)

cards.front: How can you tell a substance is IMPURE from its melting graph?
cards.back:
It melts over a range of temperatures (sloped line)

(Impure substances melt over a RANGE of temperatures, so the 'flat' part slopes upwards.)

cards.front: What is a solute?
cards.back:
The substance that dissolves in a liquid to form a solution

(Solute = the thing that dissolves [e.g. salt].)
cards.hint: Salt in salty water is the…

cards.front: What is a solvent?
cards.back:
The liquid that the solute dissolves into

(Solvent = the liquid doing the dissolving [e.g. water].)

cards.front: Write a definition for a solution.
cards.back:
The mixture formed when a solute dissolves in a solvent

(Solute + solvent = solution. Salt + water = salt solution.)

cards.front: What does SOLUBLE mean?
cards.back:
It will dissolve

(Soluble = will dissolve. INsoluble = will NOT dissolve [sand is insoluble].)

cards.front: What do we call a solution that can't take any more solute?
cards.back:
Saturated

(Saturated = no more solute will dissolve.)

cards.front: What happens to the solubility of solids as temperature goes up?
cards.back:
It increases

(Hotter water dissolves more solid. In your experiment, hot water dissolved 12 scoops of salt and cold dissolved 9.)

cards.front: In the 'temperature vs salt' experiment, what was the INDEPENDENT variable?
cards.back:
The temperature of the water

(Independent = the one thing WE change. Here that's water temperature.)

cards.front: In the same experiment, what was the DEPENDENT variable?
cards.back:
How much salt dissolved

(Dependent = what we measure or find out: how much salt dissolved.)

cards.front: In the same experiment, what was a CONTROL variable?
cards.back:
Volume of water

(Control variables are kept the same so the test is fair, e.g. same volume of water.)

cards.front: How do you make sure a practical is a fair test?
cards.back:
Only change one thing and keep everything else the same

(Change only the independent variable; keep the control variables the same.)

cards.front: Best way to separate iron filings from flour?
cards.back:
Magnet

(Iron is magnetic, flour isn't, so the iron is attracted to the magnet.)

cards.front: Best way to separate sand from water?
cards.back:
Filtration (funnel + filter paper)

(Filtration separates an INSOLUBLE solid [sand] from a liquid.)

cards.front: When you filter a mixture, what gets stuck in the filter paper?
cards.back:
The residue

(Residue = solid left behind in the paper. Filtrate = liquid that passes through.)

cards.front: What does filter paper have in it to let liquid through?
cards.back:
Tiny holes

(Small particles pass through the tiny holes; bigger solid bits can't.)

cards.front: What is the correct order to get pure salt from rock salt?
cards.back:
Crush → add water and stir → filter → evaporate

(Crush, dissolve the salt in water, filter out the rock [residue], then evaporate the salt solution [filtrate] to get crystals.)

cards.front: What process would you use to get salt crystals out of seawater?
cards.back:
Evaporation and crystallisation

(Salt is dissolved, so filtering won't work. Heat to drive off the water, then let the salt crystallise.)

cards.front: When crystallising salt, why do you stop heating when about half the water has gone?
cards.back:
So the crystals can form slowly – heating too fast spoils them

(Leaving it to crystallise slowly gives proper crystals. Heating too fast breaks them down. Then pat dry with paper towel.)

cards.front: Liquid → gas is called… and gas → liquid is called…
cards.back:
Evaporation; condensation

(Evaporation = liquid to gas. Condensation = gas to liquid [like a cold window steaming up].)
cards.hint: These two are easy to swap round!

cards.front: What did we use chromatography to separate?
cards.back:
The different dyes/pigments in inks

(Paper chromatography separates the pigments in inks, dyes and food colourings.)

cards.front: Why do we draw the start line in PENCIL in chromatography?
cards.back:
Pencil won't dissolve and run up the paper like ink would

(Ink would dissolve in the water and spread, messing up the results. Pencil [graphite] stays put.)

cards.front: Why are the ink spots kept ABOVE the water level?
cards.back:
So the ink doesn't just dissolve into the water in the beaker

(If the spots sit under the water, the ink washes into the beaker instead of travelling up the paper.)

cards.front: On a chromatogram, mixture M has spots at the same heights as dyes 1, 4 and 5. What does this tell you?
cards.back:
M contains dyes 1, 4 and 5

(Spots that line up horizontally are the same dye. M has 3 spots, so it's a mixture of 3 dyes. [The paper is called a chromatogram.])

cards.front: How is iron sulfide different from a mixture of iron and sulfur?
cards.back:
The mixture can be separated with a magnet; iron sulfide is chemically bonded, so it can't and it isn't magnetic

(Mixture: yellow powder with black specks, iron can be pulled out with a magnet. Compound [after heating]: a dark lump, a new substance, chemically bonded and hard to separate.)

cards.front: What units do we use to measure mass?
cards.back:
g or kg

(Mass = grams [g] or kilograms [kg].)
